topic.topicDisplayName: Azathioprine in rheumatic disease: TPMT testing, dosing, bone marrow suppression
topic.coverageNote: CPIC states azathioprine dosing from TPMT and NUDT15 genotypes and the myelosuppression risk in poor metabolizers. It explicitly extrapolates pharmacokinetic dosing to non-malignant immunologic disorders, which includes rheumatic use. NICE Crohn's guidance that mentions thiopurines was rejected as the wrong disease.

mcqs.question: What starting dose does CPIC recommend for TPMT normal metabolizers if a thiopurine is used?

options.D: A dose reserved for poor metabolizers

mcqs.explanation: CPIC says full starting doses are recommended for TPMT normal metabolizers.

sourceRefs.excerpt: full starting doses are recommended for TPMT normal metabolizers

mcqs.question: What dose range does CPIC give for TPMT intermediate metabolizers?

options.C: The same marked reduction used for poor metabolizers in every case
options.D: Thiopurines are contraindicated in all intermediate metabolizers

mcqs.explanation: CPIC recommends reduced doses, 30–80% of the target dose, in TPMT intermediate metabolizers.

sourceRefs.excerpt: reduced doses (30–80% of target dose) in TPMT intermediate metabolizers

mcqs.question: Why are conventional thiopurine doses dangerous in people with two loss-of-function TPMT alleles?

options.A: They are at very high risk of life-threatening myelosuppression
options.B: They clear the drug so quickly that it never works
options.C: The only risk named is hypertension
options.D: Myelosuppression is less likely than in normal metabolizers

mcqs.explanation: CPIC states that homozygous or compound heterozygous TPMT-deficient individuals are at very high risk for life-threatening myelosuppression if given conventional doses.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Individuals who inherit two loss-of-function TPMT alleles (homozygous or compound heterozygous TPMT deficient individuals) are at very high risk for life-threatening myelosuppression

mcqs.question: What does CPIC add about NUDT15?

options.A: Loss-of-function alleles reduce degradation of active thiopurine nucleotides and also predispose to myelosuppression, so poor metabolizers need substantially reduced doses or another agent
options.B: NUDT15 testing replaces the need to think about infection
options.C: NUDT15 poor metabolizers should receive higher than usual doses

mcqs.explanation: CPIC says NUDT15 loss-of-function alleles, common in Asians and Hispanics, reduce degradation of active thiopurine nucleotide metabolites and predispose to myelosuppression. Poor metabolizers need substantially reduced doses or an alternative agent.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Loss-of-function alleles in the NUDT15 gene are common in Asians and Hispanics and reduces the degradation of active thiopurine nucleotide metabolites, also predisposing to myelosuppression.

mcqs.question: Does CPIC limit these genotype recommendations to malignant disease?

options.A: No. Azathioprine and mercaptopurine are described for non-malignant immunologic disorders, and dosing is extrapolated across conditions because the association is pharmacokinetic
options.B: Yes. The guideline forbids use in rheumatic disease
options.C: Azathioprine is not a thiopurine in this text

mcqs.explanation: CPIC says mercaptopurine and azathioprine are generally used for non-malignant immunologic disorders, that azathioprine is a prodrug for mercaptopurine, and that doses are extrapolated to all conditions because the genotype association is pharmacokinetic.

sourceRefs.excerpt: mercaptopurine and azathioprine are generally used for non-malignant immunologic disorders
